resources.title: Cell structures
resources.summary: An animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterium, each drawn and labelled with the parts the specification names, plus the cytoplasm and the bacterial cell wall, and a table of what each part does and which cells have it.

visual.alt: An animal cell drawn as a rounded blob, labelled nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes and cytoplasm, each label joined by a line to its part
A plant cell drawn as a rectangle with a thick cell wall, labelled cell wall, cell membrane, chloroplasts, nucleus, ribosomes, a large vacuole and mitochondria
A bacterial cell drawn as a capsule, labelled cell wall, cell membrane, chromosomal DNA as a loose loop, two small rings of plasmid DNA, ribosomes and a whip-like flagellum

blocks.title: What each part does
rows: holds the genetic material that controls the cell
controls what enters and leaves the cell
where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose, using oxygen
where most of the cell's chemical reactions happen
strengthens and supports the cell; cellulose in a plant
holds cell sap, a watery store of sugars and salts, and keeps the cell firm
one loop of DNA, loose in the cytoplasm, not in a nucleus
small extra rings of genes, such as for resistance to an antibiotic
spins to move the bacterium along
blocks.note: Animal and plant cells are **eukaryotic**: their DNA is in a nucleus. Bacteria are **prokaryotic**: no nucleus, and much smaller.

applications.title: Antibiotics
applications.body: Antibiotics kill bacteria without harming your own cells. Some attack the bacterial cell wall, which your cells do not have. Others block bacterial ribosomes, which are built differently from yours.

applications.title: Genetic engineering
applications.body: Scientists put a human gene into a bacterial plasmid, and the bacteria then make the human protein. Insulin for people with diabetes can be made this way.

resources.title: The heart and circulation
resources.summary: The heart's four chambers, the four major blood vessels and the valves, drawn as the double circulation, with the route the blood takes and why the walls differ in thickness.

visual.alt: The double circulation: the four chambers of the heart between the lungs above and the body below, with the vena cava and pulmonary artery carrying blue deoxygenated blood on the heart's right side and the pulmonary vein and aorta carrying red oxygenated blood on its left, valves between the atria and ventricles, and the left ventricle drawn with the thickest wall

blocks.title: The four vessels
blocks.note: **Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.** The pulmonary artery is the one artery with deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein the one vein with oxygenated blood.

blocks.body:
**The route.** Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. The blood passes through the heart **twice** on each lap: that is the **double circulation**.

**The valves.** A valve is a flap that lets blood through one way and then shuts, so blood cannot flow backwards. There is one between each atrium and the ventricle below it, and one at the start of the pulmonary artery and of the aorta. The drawing shows the first pair.

**The walls.** The two upper chambers are the atria (one is an atrium). They have thin walls: they only push blood into the ventricle below. The **left ventricle has the thickest wall**, because it pumps blood all round the body. The right ventricle's wall is thinner than that, because it pumps only to the lungs, close by.

**Three kinds of vessel.** Arteries have thick, stretchy walls, because the blood in them is at high pressure. Veins have thinner walls and valves, because the pressure is low. Capillaries have walls one cell thick, so substances can pass between the blood and the cells.

**Cardiac output** is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute. **Stroke volume** is the volume pumped in one beat. **Heart rate** is the number of beats each minute. $\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$. At rest, $70$ cm³ a beat $\times$ $72$ beats a minute is $5040$ cm³ a minute, about $5$ litres a minute.

applications.title: Taking your pulse
applications.body: Each beat you feel at your wrist is the surge of blood the left ventricle has just pushed into the aorta and on through your arteries.

applications.title: Training for sport
applications.body: Regular exercise makes the heart muscle stronger, so each beat pumps more blood. A trained athlete's resting heart rate can be below 50 beats a minute for the same cardiac output.

resources.title: Maths in biology
resources.summary: The calculations Biology asks for, each with what the letters mean and a worked example: magnification, percentage change, rates, BMI, cardiac output, surface area to volume ratio, the inverse square law, Fick's law and energy transfer efficiency.
resources.statusNote: Edexcel gives no formula sheet for Biology: Ofqual's formula sheets are for Maths, Physics and Combined Science. A question may give an equation, but learn these.

items.name: Magnification
items.symbols: Both sizes in the same unit. 1 mm = 1000 μm (micrometres). A cell is 150 μm across and measures 30 mm in a photo. 30 mm is 30 000 μm, so the magnification is $30\,000 \div 150 = 200$ times.

items.name: Area of a clear zone (Biology only)
items.symbols: A clear zone is the ring round a disc where no bacteria have grown. $r$ is its radius: measure across the zone and halve it. A zone 14 mm across has $r = 7$ mm, so its area is $\pi \times 7^2 \approx 154$ mm².

items.name: Percentage change in mass
items.symbols: A gain is positive, a loss negative. Used in the osmosis practical. A potato piece goes from 2.50 g to 2.80 g: $\dfrac{2.80 - 2.50}{2.50} \times 100 = +12\%$. One that falls from 2.50 g to 2.20 g has changed by $-12\%$.

items.name: Rate
items.symbols: Or $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$ when you time how long a reaction takes. 12 cm³ of gas in 4 minutes is $12 \div 4 = 3$ cm³ a minute. Starch gone in 40 s is a rate of $1 \div 40 = 0.025$ per second.

items.name: Waist to hip ratio
items.symbols: Both in the same unit, so the ratio has none. A waist of 80 cm and hips of 100 cm give $80 \div 100 = 0.8$.

items.name: Cardiac output
items.symbols: cm³ a minute, from cm³ a beat and beats a minute

items.name: Surface area to volume ratio
items.symbols: A cube of side 2 cm has a surface area of $6 \times 2 \times 2 = 24$ cm² and a volume of $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ cm³, so the ratio is $3 : 1$. A cube of side 4 cm has $96 : 64$, which is $1.5 : 1$. The bigger the organism, the smaller the ratio.

items.name: Inverse square law
items.symbols: $\propto$ means 'is proportional to'. $d$ is the distance from the lamp. Double the distance and the intensity is a quarter: from 10 cm to 20 cm it falls to $\dfrac{1}{2^2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ of what it was.

items.name: Fick's law (Biology only)
items.formula: $\text{rate of diffusion} \propto \dfrac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness of membrane}}$
items.symbols: $\propto$ means 'is proportional to'. Double the surface area, or the concentration difference, and the rate doubles. Double the thickness of the membrane and the rate halves.

items.name: Efficiency of energy transfer (Biology only)
items.formula: $\dfrac{\text{energy in the next level}}{\text{energy in the level before}} \times 100$
items.symbols: A level is a trophic level: one step in a food chain. If the grass holds 5000 kJ and the rabbits that eat it hold 500 kJ, the efficiency is $\dfrac{500}{5000} \times 100 = 10\%$.

applications.title: Checking a microscope photo
applications.body: A red blood cell is about 8 μm across. If it measures 40 mm, which is 40 000 μm, in a photo, the magnification is $40\,000 \div 8 = 5000$ times.

applications.title: Doctors and BMI
applications.body: A person of 70 kg and 1.75 m has a BMI of $70 \div 1.75^2 \approx 22.9$, in the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9 that doctors use for adults. For anyone under 18, doctors use a chart by age instead.

resources.title: Core practicals
resources.summary: The eight core practicals in Edexcel Biology: what each investigates, what you change and what you measure. Two, marked B, are Biology only.

blocks.title: The eight core practicals
rows: the specimen on the slide and the objective lens you view it with
the image size, to work out magnification; a labelled drawing
the pH of the solution the amylase is in (a buffer solution holds the pH steady)
how long amylase takes to break down starch, tested with iodine

the result of each test. Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch. Benedict's solution, heated in a water bath, turns from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick red with reducing sugars. The biuret test turns from blue to purple with protein. The emulsion test (shake with ethanol, then pour into water) turns cloudy white with fats.
the concentration of the sucrose (sugar) solution
the percentage change in mass of potato pieces
the antibiotic, antiseptic or plant extract
the area of the clear zone round each disc, where no bacteria have grown
the distance from the lamp to the algal balls (or pondweed)
the rate of photosynthesis at each distance: how long the indicator round the algal balls takes to change colour, or the bubbles of oxygen from pondweed in a minute
the temperature of the water bath, with small organisms in a respirometer (a sealed tube joined to a thin tube of coloured liquid)
how far the coloured liquid moves in a set time, which shows how much oxygen the organisms used
where you sample along a belt transect, a line laid from one habitat into another, such as from shade into open ground
how many of each organism are inside a quadrat, a square frame, at each point along the line
blocks.note: Questions on the written papers draw on these, so know the method, the variables to control and the hazards of each.

applications.title: Hospital labs
applications.body: Practical 5.18B is like a test hospital labs use to find which antibiotic will work on a patient's infection. Discs of different antibiotics go on a plate of the bacteria. A wide clear zone, where no bacteria grow, shows that antibiotic stops them.

applications.title: Conservation surveys
applications.body: Ecologists use quadrats and belt transects to measure how plants change from a woodland edge into a field, as practical 9.5 does across a school field.
